## Estimation

This lecture is based on @maindonald book chapter 4, and @pestman

A **population parameter** is a summary of some aspect of the whole population.

We will play with a very simple data set found at <https://www.worlddata.info/average-bodyheight.php>

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(readr)
world_data_combined<-read_csv("Data_sets/world_data_combined.csv", 
    col_types = cols(...2 = col_skip(), ...6 = col_skip()))
colnames(world_data_combined)<-c("Country","Male.Height",
                                 "Male.Weight","Male.BMI",
                                 "Female.Height","Female.Weight",
                                 "Female.BMI")
```

We know that the height distribution is normally distributed, and we will find the **mean height in men** and denote that by $\mu_M$. We will assume that this is the **population parameter** (which we normally don't have).

```{r,echo=TRUE}
mu.m<-mean(world_data_combined$Male.Height)
mu.m
```

And the best estimate of the standard deviation $\sigma_M$ (as population parameter) is

```{r,echo=TRUE}
sigma.m<-sd(world_data_combined$Male.Height)
sigma.m
```

## Small sample estimation

If we are conducting an experiment in say 10 countries. We will have an estimate of this height in males $\hat{\mu}_{10}$

```{r,echo=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(require(dplyr))
```

```{r,echo=TRUE}
my.sample<-world_data_combined %>% slice_sample(n=10)
```

Now, my estimate of the average height in males will be

```{r,echo=TRUE}
mu.10<- mean(my.sample$Male.Height)
mu.10
```

How confident am I that this is a good estimate for the $\mu_M$?

Let's assume that your interest is geographically located in a region in Asia

```{r,echo=TRUE}
my.countries<-c("East Timor","Bangladesh",
                "Brunei","Laos","Philipines",
                "Madagascar","Nepal","Maynmar",
                "Indonesia","Sri Lanka","Cambodia")
my.countries.df<-world_data_combined %>% 
  filter(Country %in% my.countries)
my.countries.mu<-mean(my.countries.df$Male.Height)
my.countries.mu
```

## Assessment of accuracy

The **standard error** is defined as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the statistic. In our simple case, the statistic is the mean but it is very common so it is called **standard error of the mean (SEM)**.

If the data values are independent, an estimate of the SEM is \begin{equation*}
s_{\overline{x}}= \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\end{equation*}

The $s$ represents an estimate of the standard deviation $\sigma_M$.

The SEM indicates the extent to which the sample mean might be expected to vary from one sample to another.

Let's see with our sample of 10, and calculate the SEM

```{r,echo=TRUE}
s.10<-sigma.m/sqrt(10)
s.10
```

> Note that this number is for samples of size 10.

A small value of SEM suggests that the sample mean might be quite close to the population mean.

### Simulation with samples of size 10

```{r}
all.male.data<-world_data_combined$Male.Height
size.10.samples.mean<-rep(0,40)
for( i in 1:40){
  size.10.samples.mean[i]<-mean(sample(all.male.data,10))
}
hist(size.10.samples.mean)
```

### Simulation with samples of size 5

```{r}
size.5.samples.mean<-rep(0,40)
for( i in 1:40){
  size.5.samples.mean[i]<-mean(sample(all.male.data,5))
}
hist(size.5.samples.mean)
```

## Standardization

A very common technique in statistics is to **standardize** our data. We use the formula

\begin{equation*}
t= \frac{\overline{x}-\mu}{\text{SEM}}
\end{equation*}

The value of $t$ counts up the number of standard error units between the **true value** $\mu$ and the sample estimate $\overline{x}$; it can be thought of as a standardized distance between the **true mean** and the sample mean.

## The $t$-statistic

The variability of $t$ has 2 sources:

- the sampling variability of $\overline{x}$
- the sampling variability of SEM

Moreover, it depends on the degrees of freedom associated with the denominator (SEM)

> For a population of size $n$, we need $n-1$ degrees of freedom to estimate the standard deviation (after computing the mean)

The shape of the $t$-statistic varies with the degrees of freedom.

## Useful calculations

When we plot the probability density function, we know that the area under the curve represents a probability estimation.

![](Figures/fig_density.png)

Our goal is to calculate the area under the density curve within some specified number of standard errors in *both sides* of the mean.

More specifically, what distance from the mean gives a given probability (say 95%)? Note that 1-0.025=0.975, and 0.025 is half of the 5% (since the distribution is symmetric).

- Normal distribution $N(0,1)$. In this case, we find out the value by using the following code.

```{r,echo=TRUE}
critical.n<-qnorm(0.975)

```

The function *qnorm* makes the calculations for the normal distribution. The value `{r} critical.n`

## Interpretation

Based on the previous calculations, we can make statements such as the following

In a sample of $n=6$ observations $(x_1,\ldots, x_6)$ independent and normally distributed, there is a 95% probability that the statistic $t_5= \frac{\overline{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{6}}$ lie between (- `{r} critical_t`, `{r} critical_t`)

Or

In 95% of the samples, their average $\overline{x}$ will lie within a distance of $2.57 s/\sqrt{6}$ away from the true mean $\mu$.

## Confidence intervals

In the previous example, we write

$$P\left( -2.57  \le \frac{\overline{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{6}} \le 2.57
\right) = 0.95$$ The number 0.95 is referred to as **confident coefficient**. If we rewrite the above expression as

$$P\left(  \overline{x} -2.57 \frac{s}{\sqrt{6}} \le \mu \le  \overline{x}+2.57 \frac{s}{\sqrt{6}}
\right) = 0.95$$ The 95% **confidence interval** refers to the interval estimation of the parameter $\mu$, in this case $( \overline{x} -2.57 \frac{s}{\sqrt{6}} , \overline{x}+2.57 \frac{s}{\sqrt{6}} )$.

## A comparison table

We often require the critical values (as above the -2.57). Here is a short table to show some of those values.

| Symmetrical Probability | One-sided Probability | N(0,1) distribution | $t_8$ distribution |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 68.3% | 84.1% | 1 | 1.07 |
| 95% | 97.5% | 1.96 | 2.31 |
| 99% | 99.5% | 2.58 | 3.36 |
| 99.9% | 99.95% | 3.29 | 5.04 |

## A simulation

```{r,echo=TRUE}
set.seed(2024)
mysample<-rnorm(9,30,5)
s<-sd(mysample)
mymu<-mean(mysample)
my.crit<-2.31
low.bound<-mymu - my.crit*s/sqrt(9)
up.bound<-mymu + my.crit*s/sqrt(9)
```

We know that with probability of 95% the real mean will be between (`{r} low.bound`,`{r} up.bound`). The real mean was 30.

What happens when you remove the seed?

## Requirements for hypothesis testing

- Data (random sample)
- Statistic (a special type of function)
- A value (called the level of significance)
- A (null) hypothesis $H_0$

## Hypothesis testing

A **statistical hypothesis** $H$ is a conjecture about the probability distribution of a population.

$H_0$ is called the *null hypothesis* (for historical reasons) and $H_1$ the *alternative hypothesis*.

We say that we commit a *type I error* if we decide to accept $H_1$, whereas in reality $H_0$ is true. The probability of committing a type I error will be denoted by $\alpha$.

Acceptance of $H_0$ whereas $H_1$ is true is called a **type II error**.

The probability of committing a type II error will be denoted by $\beta$.

## Types of Errors

![](Figures/fig_hypothesis_table.png)

## Test statistics

Suppose we are dealing with a $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$-distributed population where both $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are unknown. We have collected a sample within this population of $n$ independent measures $x_1,\ldots, x_n$. If we wish to test the hypothesis $$      H_0 \colon \mu=\mu_0 \text{ against } H_1 \colon \mu\ne \mu_0
    $$ And we have calculated from that sample $s^2= \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i -\overline{x})^2$.

The outcome of the variable

$$      T= \frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} $$

is decisive in the choice to reject $H_0$ or not. This is called the **test statistic** for this hypothesis test. Under the $H_0$ the test statistics is $t$-distributed with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

The decision becomes

If\
$$\frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} < -c  \quad \text{ or } \quad \frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} > c$$ then assume $H_1$.

If $$-c \le \frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} < c$$ then, we assume $H_0$.

## p-values

The expression known as the level of significance $\alpha$ will help us to find the critical value $c$. $$      \alpha= P\left(\left|\frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\right|\ge c\right)
    $$ Then, for a given outcome of the tests statistic is $u$, the $p$-value associated is given by the quantity

$$      P\left(\left|\frac{\overline{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\right|\ge |u|\right)
    $$

## Rule based on p-values

- If $p$-value is $\le \alpha$, then assume $H_1$
- If $p$-values is $\ge \alpha$, then assume $H_0$.

"A small p-value makes the null hypothesis appear implausible. But note that it is not a probability statement about the null hypothesis itself, or for that matter about its alternative. All it offers is an assessment of implications that flow from accepting the null hypothesis. "

### P-values analog in criminal trials

> If the defendant is innocent, what is the chance that we would observe such extreme criminal evidence?

## Confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for $t$-distribution

We may be comparing one sample or differences between two samples.

|   | Confidence interval | Test statistic | Degrees of freedom |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| One-sample | $\overline{X}\pm t_{crit} SE(\overline{X})$ | $t= \frac{\overline{X}}{SE(\overline{X})}$ | $n-1$ |
| Two-sample (equal SD) | $\overline{X}_2-\overline{X}_1 \pm t_{crit} SE(\overline{X}_2-\overline{X}_1 )$ | $t= \frac{\overline{X}_2-\overline{X}_1 }{SE(\overline{X}_2-\overline{X_1} )}$ | $n_1+n_2-2$ |
| Two-sample (unequal SD) | $\overline{X}_2-\overline{X}_1 \pm t_{crit} SED$ | $t= \frac{\overline{X}_2-\overline{X}_1 }{SED}$ | $n_1+n_2-2$ |

where $SED= \sqrt{ \frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+ \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$
